parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin ā posteriōrī (literally “from what follows”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ā priōrī (“involving reasoning from cause to effect; from first principles”, literally “from the former”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin abbreviātūra.
From Medieval Latin adaptātiō, from Latin adaptare (“to adjust, fit”).
From Medieval Latin advocātūra.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin agenda. Doublet of Agenda.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin agglomerātiō, from agglomerō (“mass together”).

parole.significato: columbine (any plant of the genus Aquilegia)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ageleie, from Old High German ageleia, agaleia, agleia, acoleia, akileia (9ᵗʰ century) from the obscure Medieval Latin aquilegia which became translingual Aquilegia.

parole.significato: to accentuate, to emphasize, to accent
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin accentuare.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin algorismus, influenced by Ancient Greek ἀριθμός (arithmós).
From Medieval Latin alimentare, from Latin alimentum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin alcohol, ultimately from Arabic الكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin āreāle, neuter of āreālis.

From Medieval Latin aristocratia, from Ancient Greek ἀριστοκρατίᾱ (aristokratíā, “the rule of the best“, that is, “the best-born”, “nobility”), equivalent to Ancient Greek ἄριστος (áristos, “best”) + -kratie.

From Middle High German armbrust (12th century, variants armbrost, armborst, armbrast, armbst), from Medieval Latin arbalista, from Late Latin arcuballista, from Latin arcus (“bow”) + ballista (“ancient military engine for hurling missiles”) (compare English arbalest); modified, possibly by folk ety
Borrowed from Medieval Latin arrestum, apparently a borrowing from Old French arest.

parole.significato: one who performs physical tricks in a circus or similar context, e.g. a wirewalker, trapezist, or juggler
parole.testo: Early 14th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin artista (“artist”). The modern meaning “circus player” developed in the 19th century under influence from French artiste.

parole.significato: A man successfully reached the Bakkalaureat title.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin baccalaureus.

parole.significato: bailiwick (largest territorial division of a chivalric order, e.g. the Teutonic Order or the Order of Saint John)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin ballia + -ei.
From Middle High German basiliske, from Medieval Latin basiliscus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin bēstiārium.

parole.significato: A soft gingerbread cookie filled with almond paste from the Appenzell region in Switzerland.
parole.testo: From Middle High German bimënt, from Medieval Latin pīgmentum, explained via folk etymology from Biber (“beaver”).

parole.significato: Any of various plants in the genus Pimpinella.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pimpinella. Doublet of Pimpinelle.

From Middle High German bire, bir, from Old High German bira, pira, from Vulgar Latin pira, reanalysis of the plural of Latin pirum. Early Modern German birn is from the Middle High German plural and dative/genitive singular, whence a double plural birnen was formed. The contemporary Birne is a new
From Middle High German blīde, from Medieval Latin blida. The undiphthongised form may be of dialectal origin, but was probably reinforced by learned influence.
From Middle High German boretsch, buretsch, which reflects a Romance language pronunciation of Medieval Latin borāgō. Compare French bourrache.

parole.significato: accentor (bird of the genus Prunella), especially the dunnock (Prunella modularis)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin brunella, from Old High German brūn (“brown”) + Latin -ella.
From Middle High German bulle, from Medieval Latin bulla (“seal capsule”, literally “ball, bullet”).

Recorded circa 1840, from Christus (“Christ”) + Monogramm (“monogram”). Derived from the Medieval Latin monogramma Christi. Older literature uses the Latin expression, or Chrismon. First attested in the 18th century.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin defensivus, from Latin dēfendō.

parole.significato: to decant (to pour off (a liquid) gently, so as not to disturb the sediment)
parole.testo: Borrowed from French décanter + -ieren, from Medieval Latin dēcanthāre, from Latin canthus (“beak of a cup or jug”).
From Medieval Latin dentālis.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin discantus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diversificāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin diēta.
From Medieval Latin doctōrātus.
From Medieval Latin doxologia, from Ancient Greek δοξολογία (doxología, “a praising”).

From Middle High German dromedār (also drummeldar, trummeltier etc.), from Medieval Latin dromedarius (in part through Old French dromedaire), derived from Ancient Greek δρομάς (dromás, “running”). Doublet of Trampeltier.

parole.significato: potion (liquid which is medicinal and/or magical)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin elixir, from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “medicinal powder”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin epocha.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin exhumō, from Latin ex- + humō (“to bury”), + -ieren.
From Medieval Latin exorcizō, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō, “to banish an evil spirit; bind by oath”), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos).
From Medieval Latin excentricus, compare eccentros, ἔκκεντρος (ékkentros).

15th century, at first predominantly in the form fochen. Usually derived from Medieval Latin focō, itself from Latin focus (“hearth”). The -ch- is problematic, however. If it were due to the High German consonant shift, the word would have to be 700 years older than its first attestation. It should
Borrowed from Medieval Latin factotum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin febrilis, from Latin febris.
From feudal + -ismus [early 19th century], from Medieval Latin feudālis, from Latin feudum n (“fief, fee”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin poledrus (“a sharp-edged frame on which the suspect's feet were weighed down”), from Ancient Greek πῶλος (pôlos, “foal”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin frontispicium, possibly influenced by French frontispice.

15th century, from Futter (“lining”, formerly also “sheath”) + -al. Said to have been formed after Medieval Latin fotrale, but this is sparsely attested and no earlier than the German; thus perhaps inspired by Middle French fourrel, from Old French forrel (11th c.). All words ultimately derive from
From earlier Galgan with intrusive /t/, from Middle High German galgan, from Medieval Latin galganum, galgana, galanga.
Derived from Medieval Latin calamīna (or some Romance dialect), from Latin cadmia, ultimately from the Ancient Greek κᾰδμείᾱ, κᾰδμήᾱ, κᾰδμῐ́ᾱ (kădmeíā, kădmḗā, kădmĭ́ā, “calamine”).

From Middle High German grānāt which was borrowed from Medieval Latin granatus, most likely a substantivized masculine form of *lapis granatus.. More at Granatapfel. The term Granat in the sense of shrimp was borrowed from Middle Low German garner, garnat or garnol, itself borrowed from Middle Dutch
From Middle High German groppe, from Old High German groppo, probably from Medieval Latin corabus (“carp”), presumably a variant of or related to carabus (“crayfish”).

parole.significato: groschen; any of a number of (chiefly obsolete) coins with a related name
parole.testo: From Middle High German grosse, from Medieval Latin (denarius) grossus (“thick (penny)”).
From Middle High German gummi (13th c.), from Medieval Latin gummi, byform of older cummi(s), which see.

parole.significato: bugle, bugleweed (any of various species in the genus Ajuga)
parole.testo: From late Middle High German gunsel, from Middle High German cunsele, from Medieval Latin consolida.

parole.significato: halo (circular band of coloured light, visible around the Sun or Moon etc., caused by reflection and refraction of ligh…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin halo, from accusative of Latin halos, from Ancient Greek ἅλως (hálōs, “disk of the sun or moon; ring of light around the sun or moon; threshing floor with its surrounding threshold; disk of a shield”).

parole.significato: hermetic (completely sealed, blocking passage of any substance)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin hermeticus + -isch.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin hierarcha.
From Medieval Latin haeresis, from Ancient Greek αἵρεσις (haíresis, “taking, receiving; choice”).
From Medieval Latin haereticus (from Ancient Greek αἱρετῐκός (hairetĭkós)) + -isch.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin identitās (“sameness, identity”) in the 18th century, from Latin īdem (“the same”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin illegalis.

parole.significato: registration, addition to the register of students (at a school)
parole.testo: From immatrikulieren, from Medieval Latin immātrīculāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin immātrīculāre.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin in flagrante delicto; from Latin in + flagrō (“to burn”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin inclusivus.
From Medieval Latin intabulātiō, from tabula (“tablet”).
From Medieval Latin interesse under influence of French intérêt.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intrūsiō, from Latin intrūdō.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin intuitiō.
Ultimately from Medieval Latin invectīva (“invective, abusive speech”), neuter plural of Latin invectīvus, from invehō (“to carry in”). Compare English inveigh.
Medieval Latin investītūra

From Medieval Latin Jōhannēs, from Late Latin Iōhannēs, variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān) (perhaps from a former J^əhôħānān). Cognate with English John.
From Middle High German juriste, borrowed from Medieval Latin jurista.

parole.significato: judiciary; judicial system; judicial authorities and procedures; justice (in this sense)
parole.testo: 16th c., from Medieval Latin iūstitia (“justice, judiciary, jurisdiction”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin caldūna. Compare Old French chaudun, source of English chawdron.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin calīphātus. By surface analysis, Kalif + -at.

parole.significato: camomile (plant of the genus Matricaria, particularly Matricaria recutita, German chamomile)
parole.testo: Middle High German gamille, Medieval Latin camomilla.
From Middle High German kampfer, from Medieval Latin camphora, nasalized byform of cafora, from Arabic كَافُور (kāfūr), from an Austronesian language (cf. Malay kapur).
From Middle High German kaplān, kappelān, from Medieval Latin cappellānus.
Middle High German, from Medieval Latin carnārium.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin cassatio.

From Middle High German kelnære, from Old High German kelnere, from Medieval Latin cellenarius (“(wine) cellar administrator”), from Late Latin cellārium (“pantry”), with influence of Keller, itself ultimately from the same Latin source.

From Middle High German ketzer, from Old High German ketzer, kether, from Medieval Latin Catharī, from Byzantine Greek Καθαροί (Katharoí), substantive form of Ancient Greek καθαρός (katharós, “pure”). Doublet of Katharer. See English Cathar.
From Late Latin clēricus + -ei, perhaps via Medieval Latin clēricia.

parole.significato: a kind of voluminous head finery (Kopfputz) of varying appearance throughout the centuries and regions but later more o…
parole.testo: From Middle High German gugele, gugel, kugel, kogel, from Old High German cugula, chugela, cucala, from Medieval Latin cuculla.
From Middle High German kolre, from Old High German koloro, from Medieval Latin cholera (“outburst of anger”), from Latin cholera (“bile, anger”). Doublet of Cholera. Cognate with English choler.

parole.significato: an ecclesiastical benefice transferred in trust to the custody of a patron
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin commenda.

parole.significato: commander, knight commander (of a basic administrative division called Kommende or Komturei)
parole.testo: Possibly through or influenced by Medieval Latin commendatarius (“commendatary”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin conditiō, from Latin condiciō.
Middle High German confect, Medieval Latin cōnfectum.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin concordantia.

parole.significato: concordat (formal agreement between a nation and the Vatican)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin concordatum, from Latin concordāre (“to agree”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin connotātiō, from Latin connotō.

parole.significato: consecutive (expressing the consequence of an action)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin cōnsecūtīvus, in part through French consécutif.

parole.significato: counterpoint (melody added to an existing one)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin contrapunctum.
Medieval Latin convolūtum

parole.significato: to coordinate, to harmonize (to handle in a centralized and systematic way)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin coordinare + -ieren.

parole.significato: to correlate (to be related by a correlation)
parole.testo: Back-formation from Korrelation, from Medieval Latin correlātiō, suffixed with -ieren.
From Middle High German koste, kost. From Medieval Latin costus, costa. Ultimately from the Latin verb constare. Older singular forms were found in Kost f, Koste f, Kost m, and Kosten m.
From Middle High German kunkel, from Medieval Latin conucla, conucula, colucula, corrupted from Latin colus (“distaff”).

parole.significato: habit (a long piece of clothing worn by monks and nuns)
parole.testo: From Middle High German kutte (“monk habit”), from Medieval Latin cotta (“undercoat, tunic”), from Proto-Germanic *kuttô (“cowl, woolen cloth, coat”).

From Middle High German chafter (“beehive; little chamber, closet”), from Old High German chafteri (“beehive”), from Medieval Latin capistērium (“beehive”), for scaphistērium, from Ancient Greek σκαφιστήριον (skaphistḗrion).
From Medieval Latin labiālis.

parole.significato: laboratory (room, building or institution equipped for scientific research)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin labōrātōrium.
Middle High German lāsūr, lāsūre or lāzūr, lāzūre, from Medieval Latin lazurium, lazur, from Arabic لَازُوَرْد (lāzuward, “lapis lazuli, azure”), from Persian لاجورد (lâjvard).
From Middle High German lavendel(e), from Old High German lavendula (10th c.), from Medieval Latin lavendula.
From Lehen + -s- + Gericht, calque of Medieval Latin curia feudalis.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin linguālis, from Latin lingua (“tongue, speech”).
From Middle High German linie, from Medieval Latin linea, alternative form of older Latin līnea. Earlier borrowings from the same source, such as Old High German linna, were not continued.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin lupīnus.
From Middle High German maiorān, from Late Old High German maiolan, from Medieval Latin maiorana (“majoranus”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin maiōrennis.
From Medieval Latin mandatarius, from mandātum (“mandate”).
From Middle High German mandel, from Medieval Latin mandala (“sheaf, bundle”), which in the sense of “handful” is probably related to Latin manus (“hand”).
From Medieval Latin manifestum.
16th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin manuscrīptum.

parole.significato: moult (the process in which a bird’s plumage renews).
parole.testo: From Middle High German mūze, from Old High German mūzōn (“change, transform”), from Medieval Latin muta, from Latin mutare (“change, transform”).

parole.significato: administrator or leaseholder of a manor
parole.testo: First attested as Old High German meior (9th century). Middle High German meier or meiger. Ultimately from Medieval Latin maior (domus).
From late Middle High German metzelen, from Medieval Latin macellare (“slaughter”), from Latin macellum (“meat, meat market”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin minerāle (neuter of minerālis), from Medieval Latin minera.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin minōrennis.

parole.significato: minute (unit of time; unit of angle)
parole.testo: 15th c., from Medieval Latin minūta (“60th of an hour; note”).
From Medieval Latin moschus, alternative form of muscus, from Ancient Greek μόσχος (móskhos), from Middle Persian [script needed] (mwšk' /⁠mušk⁠⁠/).
16th century, from Medieval Latin mūsicāns, present participle of mūsicō (“to play music”), perhaps through Italian musicante. Equivalent to Musik + -ant.
From Middle High German almuʒ, ultimately from Medieval Latin almutia (“hood, cowl”), of unknown origin. Compare Latin amictus (“clothed, veiled”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin narcōticum (“narcotic”, neuter singular), from Ancient Greek ναρκωτικός (narkōtikós), from ναρκόω (narkóō, “to numb”).

From Middle High German nunne, from Old High German nunna, from Medieval Latin nonna. The -o- is the regular outcome of Middle High German -u- before a nasal geminate, though it might have been reinforced by relatinisation.

parole.significato: nuncio (diplomatic representative of the Roman Catholic Church)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nūntius.

parole.significato: An interval of 12 semitones; an octave.
parole.testo: From Middle High German octāv, from Medieval Latin octava (“eighth”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin omnipraesēns.

parole.significato: to sacrifice, to give up (for a goal or cause)
parole.testo: From Middle High German opfern, ophern, from Old High German opfarōn, opharōn, offarōn, from Medieval Latin operor (“work”) and/or Medieval Latin offerō (“offer”).
From Medieval Latin orthogonalis, from Latin orthogonius (“right-angled”).
From Medieval Latin palliātīvum, neuter singular form of palliātīvus, from Latin palliō (“I conceal”).
From Medieval Latin palliātīvus, from Latin palliō (“I conceal”).
From Medieval Latin papulus (“poplar tree”), a variant of classical Latin pōpulus; compare Dutch peppel (from Middle Dutch pappel).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin paramentum, from parō (“adorn”) + -mentum.

parole.significato: paroxysm (random or sudden outburst; explosive event during a volcanic eruption; sudden recurrence of a disease)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin paroxysmus, from Ancient Greek παροξυσμός (paroxusmós, “irritation, the severe fit of a disease”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin passus.

From Middle High German pate, bate, from Medieval Latin pāter spīrituālis. Compare Middle Low German pāde, Old High German pate (“godmother”), Middle High German pfetter (from Old High German pfetiro (“godfather”)). Related to German Pfetter.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin patriarchātus.
Middle High German pedel, from Medieval Latin pedellus, bedellus, perhaps influenced by Büttel, from Proto-Germanic *budilaz. Cognate with English bedel and beadle.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pendulum, from pendulus (“hanging”), from pendeō (“I hang”).
Borrowed from Medieval Latin pennale, from penna.
From Medieval Latin permanentia, from Latin permaneō (“to remain; last”).

parole.significato: palace (of certain mediaeval emperors and kings)
parole.testo: From Middle High German phalanze, phalenze, pfalze, from Old High German phalanza, phalinza, falenza, borrowed from Medieval Latin palantia, from palātia, from palātium.

parole.significato: benefice (income attached to an ecclesiastical function)
parole.testo: From Middle High German pfrüende, pfruonde, from Old High German phruonta, from (early) Medieval Latin provenda, alteration of Latin praebenda.
From Middle High German viole, from Medieval Latin fiola, from phiala. Doublet of Fiale.

parole.significato: Any of various plants in the genus Pimpinella.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin pimpinella. Doublet of Bibernelle.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin policia, from Late Latin polītīa.

15th century, from Medieval Latin pomerancium, from pomum (“fruit”) + arancia (“orange”), the latter from Arabic نارَنْج (nāranj), from Persian نارنگ (nârang). Doublet of Orange. Cognate with Italian pomarancia (“sweet orange”).

parole.significato: profession (promise or vow made on entering a religious order)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin professus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin prōstata, from Ancient Greek προστάτης (prostátēs, “one standing before, protector”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to stand”).
Calque of Medieval Latin provisorius, using Latin provis- (supine stem of provideo) + -orisch (“-ory”).

parole.significato: preamble (a short statement or remark, especially an explanatory introduction to a formal document or statute)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praeambulum, from Latin praeambulō. Compare German preamble.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin praediālis, from Latin praedium (“farm, estate, land”).

parole.significato: to qualify (to make someone competent or eligible)
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin quālificāre. Compare French qualifier and English qualify.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin quantifico.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin quārtāle n (literally “one fourth”).
18th century, borrowed from Medieval Latin querulāns. In its broadened sense associated with unrelated quer (“cross, diagonal”).
From Medieval Latin quinquagesima dies (“50th day”).

parole.significato: A fifth; an interval of six (kleine Quinte, diminished fifth) or seven (große Quinte, perfect fifth) semitones.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin quinta. Doublet of Quinta.
From Medieval Latin rabiatus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin ratificare, from Latin ratus (“established, authoritative; fixed, certain”) + faciō, facere (“to make”)
From Medieval Latin reagō.

parole.significato: a trainee going through preparatory service for public office (Vorbereitungsdienst) which requires successful universit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin referendarius.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin rehabilitāre.
From Reich + -s- + Apfel. Calque of Medieval Latin pomum imperiale.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin respectīvē, adverb of respectīvus.

parole.significato: responsory (chant or anthem recited after a reading in a church service)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin responsorium.

parole.significato: currant (Ribes gen. et spp., chiefly the fruits)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin ribes, ribesium, from Arabic رِيبَاس (rībās).

parole.significato: quantity of paper containing 1000 sheets (two reams)
parole.testo: From Middle High German ris, from Medieval Latin rīsma, from Arabic رِزْمَة (rizma, “bundle”). Cognate with English ream.
From Medieval Latin rigorōsus influenced by French rigoureux.
From Middle High German rūzesch, from Rūz, from Old High German Rūzo, from Medieval Latin Russus, from Byzantine Greek Ῥῶς (Rhôs). By surface analysis, Russe + -isch.

parole.significato: sacristy (room in a church where sacred vessels, books, vestments, etc. are kept)
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle High German sacristīe, from Medieval Latin sacristi|a, ~ae.

parole.significato: scholar, especially in the Middle Ages
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin scholāris.

parole.significato: pupil, student, schoolboy (male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German schuolære, from Old High German scuolāri, from Medieval Latin scholaris; analyzable as Schule + -er.
From Middle High German sīdel, borrowed in the 13th c. from Medieval Latin situlum, from Latin situla.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin sensitivus.
From Medieval Latin sēriōsitās.
Middle High German sigrist, from Medieval Latin sacrista.
From Middle High German sirup, sirop (13th c.), from Medieval Latin siruppus, siropus, from Arabic شَرَاب (šarāb, “drink”). See English syrup for more.

From Late Middle High German sklafe (15th c.), a relatinisation of older slave (13th c.), from Medieval Latin s(c)lavus, from Late Latin Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos); see that Greek entry and slave for more. Doublet of Slawe and ciao.

parole.significato: Slav (member of a Slavic people, male or of unspecified gender)
parole.testo: From Middle High German Slave, from Medieval Latin Sclavus. Distinguished from the doublet Sklave since the 18th century, probably influenced by descendants of Proto-Slavic *slověninъ. Also a doublet of ciao.
From Medieval Latin Sclavus.

From 15th-century Middle High German sparge, spargen, sparges, from Medieval Latin sparagus, asparagus, in part through Italian sparago, sparagio. The form in -el (16th c.) probably after such plant names as Kerbel, Kümmel.
Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from late Medieval Latin sparta, from Ancient Greek σπάρτη (spártē, “hereditament”).

Back-formed from the plural Spirituosen which was borrowed from Medieval Latin spīrituōsa (“spirits”), substantivized neuter plural of spīrituōsus, from spīritus. The shift from neuter to feminine gender occurred because the morph -en is characteristic for feminine plural rather than neuter.

parole.significato: a fee accepted by public officers (including judges, university professors, pastors etc.) to act in the capacity of the…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin sportula.
Late Middle High German stathalter, calque of Medieval Latin locumtenens (“lieutenant”). Compare Dutch stadhouder.

Calque of Medieval Latin stante pede (literally “with one’s foot standing still”), a medieval juridical term meaning "on the spot, without having left the court". parole.significato: student (person attending lectures at a university; male or of unspecified sex)
parole.testo: From Middle High German studente, from Medieval Latin studēns.

From Middle High German soldener, soldenier, soldenære, derived from solt (modern Sold), likely after Medieval Latin soldonerius and Old Italian soldoniere, soldaniere, literally “salaried”, derived from soldo (“sold, salary”), used in the times of feudal militias, referring to hired or enlisted pai
From Medieval Latin tamarindus, possibly via Italian tamarindo.
From Middle High German taphart, daphart, tappart, from Medieval Latin tabardum, from Old French tabard.
Coined in German from Medieval Latin taxa (“tax, charge”) and -meter.

parole.significato: fee, tariff, tax (a payment required to cover administrative costs or in exchange for a service)
parole.testo: 15th century, from Medieval Latin taxa.

parole.significato: rug, carpet (cloth covering for a floor)
parole.testo: From Middle High German teppich, tepich, teppech, tepech, tepch, teppch; from Old High German teppih, tepich, teppech; from Medieval Latin tapicus; from Latin tapes.
From Middle High German tincte, tinte, dinte, etc., from Old High German tincta, borrowed from Medieval Latin tincta, from tingō (“to wet, dip, dye, tinge”).
Old High German torcula, from Medieval Latin torcula, from torculum (“wine or olive press”).

parole.significato: total, absolute, complete, utter (not used in the sense of “entire”)
parole.testo: 16th century, from Medieval Latin tōtālis, in part through Middle French total.
From Medieval Latin transformātīvus (“transformative”).
From Medieval Latin trānsversālis, from Latin trānsversus.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin tūtōrium.
